Author: @dennisjungbauer4467
Content:
Regarding AI: I have that fear as well. Just few days ago I saw a comment on YT that the uploader should disable AA as he was using DLSS, being confident that having AA enabled will reduce performance when DLSS or the like is enabled as well. Some other commenter corrected him, but he doubled down that that's wrong and he asked ChatGPT about it.. 😶
My best friend also is a strong believer of AI and uses ChatGPT constantly, after some discussion about it, I challenged him to ask ChatGPT about sth. more niche; asking what smartphones have the best integrated DACs for listening to music with headphones (don't know how we phrased the question now) and among these, there was (at least) one that did not even have a headphone jack. 😄 Now, to my surprise, it wasn't completely wrong in theory, but the way to make it make sense is not universally applicable and, without further research, it's misleading at best. And you can probably bet how many will do further research to check if the answer makes sense.. 🥲

I made it part of my mission to fight misinformation years ago, in some cases I'm even spending an hour of research for some YT comment, and now this is the development.. 😐
Adding to that, the increasing number of bullshit sites that generate pages for every search term, AI or otherwise.. Had a fun experience last year at work, where I was searching for some unexpected error message and the first 3 search results or so where effectively the same bullshit generated content, with a believable screenshot even, but luckily my bullshit detection senses kicked in and after some more searching I found an actual correct explanation for it..

Author: @LibertyMonk
Content:
AI (LLM) Temperature tuning means that word choice is flexible, and it'll chose the option it has 10% confidence in over the option it has 40% confidence in *some* times. And this makes for better, more natural writing more often. But, picking "2020" when you're 10% sure (because, well, it's a year, and it's close to 2019) instead of "2018" which you're 80% sure (because that's what all but one sources agree is correct) is the kind of garbage only LLM summaries can be.

Getting different answers is a feature. It's an integral part of the model. The problem is it's totally willing to pick the 2nd or 3rds best "fact", even if it's very confident that the 1st best is correct. "close enough" is basically fine when you're describing the form and color of some background detail that you're not supposed to closely examine. It's usually better than just a blank wall. But "AI" designers and users need to learn the difference between important factual tokens that *should not* be high Temperature, and syntactic fluff that a synonym for is acceptable.

Whoa whoa whoa. Steve is usually spot-on but in this case regarding the Steam Deck vs Rog Ally,

“That’s potentially a hard sell for most people considering the latter (rog Ally) has * *better hardware*” and then going on to list Deck positives EXCEPT THE OLED SCREEN.

Author: @bullcompost
Content:
Something that is easy to forget when talking about AI (which stands for Artificial Idiocy or Artificial Intelligence; I don't remember which one, but there's not much difference between the two) is that AI is supposed to make computer think like humans.
How many humans (in percentage) should you trust if you ask them a specific question that requires knowledge and accuracy to be satisfactorily answered?
Ask somebody, for example, if Risk or Cisc is the best approach to developing processors, for example.
What percentage of humans would provide an answer that ends up being misleading, irrelevant, confusing or whatever else?
The real trick of AI is not to make computers think like humans. It's to make humans behave like (idiotic) computers.
It is human to make mistakes, but if you want to mess everything up, you definitely need a computer.

Author: @FromWitchSide
Content:
I have tried ChatGPT about 5 times, each time it provided me with a wrong answer. My recent questions were about CD-ROM drives where it told me Amiga 1200 had official CD-ROM drive released as A570 in 1993, however A570 is Amiga 500 only CD-ROM released in 1992, the 1200 never got one. Like wise it gave me a CD music player as a first commercially available PC CD-ROM drive, and it even got the year wrong by a margin of 3 years. When I finally forced it for a possibly (because answers were vague, and always "among the earliest" instead "the first') right model, it argued for it to be right by citing a support for the standard which was only published 3 years later, and not even formulated at the time of the drive's in question release. By changing the referenced standards along my questioning of the answers, it changed its mind down to 1 year difference, after which it said it didn't fallow any set standards. When asked about sources, it referenced some websites, but manually checking them provided no such information. When asked about it, it would admit to being wrong and just continue, and when asked about a link or a quote to the referenced online material it admitted it was wrong about the source availability (as some webpages it referenced did not exist). I also recall asking it about USB interface chips from a specific company, wanted know which of 3 models was better, and the answer was super vague indicating all were the best. I've asked it for the specs difference and comparative data 3 times, before it actually gave me that, and even then it referenced it wrong. Just googling pdf datasheets for the chips and checking them was actually faster. With each of my questions, I felt like ChatGPT is actively trying to fool me.

Those are all the questions which should be the easiest for "AI", because they are very specific, the devices, parts, specifications, years, are all specific data which can be tracked, referenced and won't have much ambiguity. Just thinking about someone asking a more vague question and running off with the answer it got from "AI", is truly a horror.

Author: @tahrey
Content:
Wait wait wait wait wait ... did you say ONE HUNDRED AND EIGHTY NANOSECOND memory latency?! That's... like... 6MHz PC/AT performance. How can it be that bad? Even yer old Amiga/ST/Mac running at about 7-8MHz used 150ns DRAMs. That's a thousand times worse than it should be. (Well, OK, maybe about 400, as they interleaved CPU and video access, but that still shows that memory has been that fast for a very long time).

Even "aiming" for 70 to 85ns seems bizarre. The first x86 PC my family had was a 486 with 70ns FPM in it, later upgraded to 60ns EDO when we entered the Pentium era.

I know DRAM latency is a big problem and something that's failed to keep pace with the actual raw transfer speeds once a burst transaction is actually set up, hence the need for multiple layers of cache that are now exceeding the full memory complement of a high-end turn-of-the-millennium PC, but I could have sworn we were at least down into the 20-30ns range by now, with early SDRAM being like 50ns or better. I wouldn't even be surprised to find high performance SSDs knocking on the door of 100ns, given the IOPS ratings.

What's the deal here? Why are they quoting numbers that I would have more expected to be used 30+ years ago, in terms of someone saying "we expected X but got Y, and that's why performance is bad"? Were they talking about cache and meant to quote picoseconds? (SRAM / registers after all have been sub-20ns for at least as long, and should be sub-nanosecond by now... that's how processors can run at >5GHz in the first place, by having fractional-ns response time, like 200ps or less... graphics systems could already produce 30ns pixels in the 1980s)

If it's true then, damn, no wonder it's causing bottlenecking if you may have to wait a good thousand clocks of a 5.5GHz core to fetch data from RAM (nevermind if you have 8 or more cores all wanting data from different places in memory). It taking a little less than half the time to do that is still pretty bad, but it potentially doubles your throughput in highly randomised fetch patterns. But I'm still puzzled by how those numbers aren't, like, 1/10th the magnitude or better. (3200MHz memory with a CL20 rating would surely be, like... 6ns latency?)

Content:
A bought the 420mm Artic Freezer III that was on sale on Newegg. While I'm happy with the purchase overall this is by far the worst cooler I have ever installed from a ease of installation perspective.  The included instructions, and the youtube video explaining the install did NOT work for me. Judging from the comments in the youtube video I was not the only one with this issue. 

A selection of comments from their video www.youtube.com/watch?v=5YbKo-Gcmbs&t=18s :

"thread the leaf spring screws into the brackets first, then apply thermal paste and set the spacers, then thread the bracket to mobo screws. tighten the bracket to mobo screws in a star pattern, when secure, finish tightening down the leaf spring screws. I literally just did these steps and it went smoothly. A beer also helps ;)"


"Install the L and R rails to the block FIRST and then install the rails to the motherboard. It will save you hours of frustration and is safer to do it that way."

"This cooler mount is the most difficult ive ever tried in 12 years of building pc's for amd. I don't understand why its so needlessly hard to get 2 screws in on a mount."

"Sorry to say but this mounting is a step down from the II, I have both now in 2 different builds and managing to screw in the pump screws onto the brackets has been HELL
At first I thought it was defective because even with just a couple turns the opposite screw kept jumping out, first time looked properly seated but wasn't, cpu went 60° steady, so remounted it, but some reason the plate was a bit rotated so I remounted it again making sure the black brackets where screwed straight, but the outcome was the same... in the end I screwed both the screws at the same time by hand, then finished with 2 screwdrivers at the same time... 

This mounting is at the same level of the old intel 775 stock cooler plastic pins, who know what I'm talking about can relate.


Cooler itself is awesome though, and being finally able to control everything is great, mounted a 360 in push pull inside a 7000D, but I guess I'll keep the pump rotated 1° to the left!"

Author: @Twilightsfavquill
Content:
Regarding the Problems that Google Search AI has: From a technical perspective, Googe Search AI utilizes Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) to build the answer to a user's query. This technology uses two large language models, an Encode and a Decoder to generate the text: The Encoder searches for relevant sources in a vector database, depending on the user query. The Decoder (Generator) then receives the original user query together with the sources retrieved by the Encoder through vector similarity search and generates an answer with this. The problem here is that the Generator is still a large language model which tends to halucinate wrong answeres, even if the correct answer was given as the input.
This behavior is of course very problematic and may lead to lots of lawsuits in the future, where "chatbots" for major companies may give erronious and outrages answers.
